passage: I'm Sahil. When Rehana admitted she had pushed a change without testing and broken the build, I could see her bracing. So I told her about the worst project of my early career: a billing module I insisted on rewriting alone, then hid my delays for weeks, and shipped late with bugs that cost a client an evening of manual work. I kept it to three minutes, no dramatic ending, because this wasn't my moment. What I learned, I said, was that telling the team early would have saved everyone time. Then I turned it back to her: 'What would you want the team to know about yesterday?' Rehana let out a breath and began to explain. Later she said it was easier to talk once she knew I had stumbled too.

qa.q: How long did Sahil's story take?
qa.a: Sahil kept it to three minutes.

qa.q: What did Sahil want to make sure of while telling the story?
qa.a: Sahil was concerned that Rehana was bracing herself, so Sahil kept the story short and turned it back to her, making sure the talk stayed about her.

qa.q: What could Sahil do if Rehana still stayed quiet about the mistake?
qa.a: Sahil could offer to go through the change together on a shared screen, since working side by side takes away some of the pressure of explaining.

qa.q: How did the story feel to Rehana?
qa.a: Rehana felt relieved and safer: she let out a breath, and later said it was easier to talk knowing Sahil had stumbled too. 🙂

grounding: Shows a mentor telling a short honest story of a past bad project and its lesson so the mentee can admit a mistake, without making the story about themselves.

passage:
Mentoring programme observation note, session 4.
I sat in on Trisha's session with her mentee, Chetan, today. For three sessions Chetan had said everything was 'fine', though his project was clearly behind. Today Trisha tried something different. She told him about her first year: a dashboard project she had promised in six weeks that took five months, and how she hid the delay until her manager heard about it from a client. She kept it to about four minutes, then turned it back to him: 'So, how's yours really going?'
Chetan was quiet, then admitted he was two weeks behind and scared to say so. They spent the rest of the hour on a plan to tell his lead.
Trisha stopped her story before it became about her, which mattered. I have suggested she keep that balance.
Programme coordinator

qa.q: How long did Trisha's dashboard project actually take?
qa.a: Five months, instead of six weeks.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling before he admitted the delay?
qa.a: Chetan was scared to admit being two weeks behind, which is why everything had been 'fine' for three sessions.

qa.q: Why did Trisha keep the story to about four minutes?
qa.a: So the session stayed about Chetan; a short story made it safe to admit mistakes without turning the focus to Trisha.

qa.q: How might Chetan's lead be affected by the plan?
qa.a: The lead will hear about the delay early from Chetan, which gives time to adjust instead of a surprise later.

grounding: It shows a coordinator's note on a mentor who shares a past failure briefly so the mentee feels safe admitting mistakes, without making the story about herself.

passage:
Thursday, 10 p.m.
Tonight I told Chinmay about the worst launch of my life: the app I released on a Friday that logged out every user in the country. I told it in five minutes, with the embarrassing bits: I cried in the parking lot, I nearly quit. Then I stopped, because I noticed I was starting to enjoy telling it.
I asked him about his week. And for the first time in two months, he didn't say 'all good'. He said he'd merged something without tests and was terrified it would break. We opened it together and added the tests.
Note to self: the story is a door, not a stage. Walk him through it, then get out of the way.
Sarita

qa.q: What did Sarita's app do when it was released on a Friday?
qa.a: It logged out every user in the country.

qa.q: Why did Sarita stop telling the story, and how did Sarita feel about it?
qa.a: Sarita felt a little uneasy on noticing a growing enjoyment in telling it, and did not want the session to become about the mentor.

qa.q: What does Sarita mean by 'the story is a door, not a stage'?
qa.a: Sharing a failure should open space for the mentee to speak, not become a performance about the mentor.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see Sarita after hearing the story?
qa.a: Chinmay may see Sarita as human and safe to be honest with, since Sarita admitted crying and nearly quitting.

grounding: It shows a mentor sharing a past bad project honestly so the mentee feels safe admitting a mistake, while keeping the focus off the mentor.
